evidence.effect: Self-assessed 89% correct versus 67% by human evaluators; chi-square, P < 0.0001.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4o-mini self-assessed 89% of responses as correct (scores 1-2), compared to 67% by human evaluators (chi-square, P < 0.0001), with the greatest discrepancy in the partially correct category.
evidence.sample_unit: AI-generated visceral aneurysm clinical scenarios and responses

evidence.title: Evaluation of Arabic-Language AI Chatbot Responses to Migraine-Related Questions: A Comparative Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.outcome: Differences between chatbots in source transparency and communication of uncertainty in Arabic migraine answers
evidence.effect: Accuracy did not differ across models (p = 0.072), but mDISCERN differed significantly (p < 0.001); clearest differences were in source transparency and communication of uncertainty.
evidence.quote: The clearest between-model differences were observed in source transparency and communication of uncertainty.

evidence.title: Comparative performance of ChatGPT and DeepSeek in interpreting the 2025 ESICM guidelines on sepsis fluid therapy
evidence.outcome: Calibrated uncertainty expression in guideline-defined uncertainty domains
evidence.effect: Models gave consistently overconfident responses in domains where the guidelines define evidence as uncertain, described as an important safety limitation.
evidence.quote: Advanced LLMs show potential for supporting sepsis fluid therapy guideline interpretation, but consistent overconfident responses in guideline-defined uncertainty domains highlight important safety limitations.
evidence.sample_unit: guideline-derived clinical questions (each queried in English and Chinese, 3 responses per model)

evidence.title: Patient-Facing Radiology Communication with LLMs: Calibration Deficit and the Metadata Paradox
evidence.outcome: Self-reported confidence among safety-critical (Score 1) LLM errors
evidence.effect: Most safety-critical errors (n = 131) were assigned high self-confidence (>=8/10): GPT-4o mini 93.8%, Grok 100%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 61.5%.
evidence.quote: notably, the majority of safety-critical errors (Score 1: clinically significant misinformation; n = 131) were assigned high self-confidence (≥8/10; GPT-4o mini: 93.8%, Grok: 100%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet: 61.5%).
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated answers to simulated patient questions

evidence.title: Assessing Readability and DISCERN Quality of Osteoporosis Education Materials Generated by ChatGPT and Deepseek for Diverse Health Literacy Levels: A Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.outcome: Explicit uncertainty statements in LLM-generated patient education (DISCERN Q8)
evidence.effect: 10 of 12 texts (83%) scored ≤2/5 on uncertainty statements; no model achieved acceptable performance on Q8.
evidence.quote: No model achieved acceptable performance on Q4, Q5, Q7, or Q8.
evidence.sample_unit: composite LLM-generated texts (4 models × 3 literacy tiers; 72 outputs aggregated)

evidence.title: Bedside Triage by Large Language Models in Acute Pancreatitis: A Scenario-Based Comparative Evaluation of GPT-4, GPT-5, and Gemini
evidence.outcome: Unwarranted certainty in outputs under missing data
evidence.effect: Unwarranted certainty under missing data occurred in 12/20 GPT-4, 7/20 GPT-5, and 15/20 Gemini outputs.
evidence.quote: All models demonstrated clinically relevant failure modes, particularly unwarranted certainty under missing data; this occurred in 12/20 GPT-4, 7/20 GPT-5, and 15/20 Gemini outputs.
evidence.sample_unit: acute pancreatitis scenarios (15 hypothetical vignettes, 5 de-identified real-case patterns)

evidence.title: Gut Instincts, Machine Decisions: Evaluating AI Accuracy in the Diagnosis and Treatment of Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction
evidence.outcome: LLM self-reported confidence ratings relative to diagnostic accuracy
evidence.effect: Confidence ratings uniformly high regardless of accuracy, mean 93% to 96% (SD 1% to 4%), while diagnostic accuracy was 65% to 74%.
evidence.quote: Confidence ratings were uniformly high regardless of accuracy, with the mean scores ranging from 93% to 96% and standard deviation ranging from 1% to 4%.

evidence.title: Between Accessibility and Reliability: High Confidence, Low Control in General-Purpose Multimodal Models for Hip Fracture Radiograph Interpretation
evidence.outcome: Whether self-reported confidence distinguished correct from incorrect outputs
evidence.effect: Both models frequently remained highly confident when wrong; self-reported confidence did not reliably distinguish correct from incorrect outputs.
evidence.quote: Both models frequently remained highly confident when wrong, and self-reported confidence did not reliably distinguish correct from incorrect outputs.
evidence.sample_unit: surgically confirmed hip fracture AP pelvis radiographs

evidence.title: Comparison of large language models in the management of pediatric ureteropelvic junction obstruction: a comparative analysis of 125 clinical scenarios
evidence.outcome: Overconfident presentation masking clinical inaccuracies in LLM outputs
evidence.effect: Copilot had highest readability (4.13 +/- 0.65) but lower accuracy (3.49 +/- 1.67); authors describe a 'readability-accuracy paradox' and 'deceptive confidence' posing misinformation risk.
evidence.quote: However, the "deceptive confidence" of models like Copilot poses a risk of misinformation.

evidence.title: Predictive accuracy of a general-purpose artificial intelligence model for cut-out following proximal femoral nailing
evidence.venue: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery
evidence.outcome: Calibration of ChatGPT predicted probabilities for correct versus incorrect classifications
evidence.effect: Calibration inverted: median predicted probability 9% for correct vs 40% for incorrect classifications (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001).
evidence.quote: Calibration was inverted: the median predicted probability was lower for correct (9%) than for incorrect (40%) classifications (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Multimodal Large Language Models for Four-Class Benchmark of Oral Autoimmune Blistering Diseases: A Multicenter Paired Study
evidence.outcome: Calibration of model confidence (Brier score, expected calibration error)
evidence.effect: Claude had lower one-vs-rest Brier score (0.0468 vs. 0.0558), whereas Gemini had lower expected calibration error (0.083 vs. 0.251); calibration was metric-dependent.
evidence.quote: Calibration results were metric-dependent: Claude had a lower one-vs-rest Brier score (0.0468 vs. 0.0558), whereas Gemini had a lower expected calibration error (0.083 vs. 0.251).

evidence.title: Performance of large language models on narrow therapeutic index drug monitoring: Implications for clinical pharmacy practice
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Pharmacists Association : JAPhA
evidence.outcome: Overconfident reasoning errors in LLM TDM responses
evidence.effect: Overconfident reasoning was the most common error category (45.4% of total error appearances); models differed significantly on uncertainty acknowledgment (Holm-adjusted p≤0.02).
evidence.quote: Overconfident reasoning was the most common error category (45.4% of total error appearances).

evidence.title: MiraMind: Benchmarking Reliable Mental Health Reasoning beyond Answer Accuracy
evidence.outcome: Whether LLM judgments' certainty and specificity exceed what limited mental-health evidence supports
evidence.effect: Across 20 LLMs, a 'restraint gap' was found: the specificity or certainty of model judgments exceeds what limited evidence supports. No numbers are given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Evaluating 20 LLMs reveals a restraint gap, in which the specificity or certainty of model judgments exceeds what limited evidence supports.

evidence.title: Faithfulness vs. Safety: Evaluating LLM Behavior Under Counterfactual Medical Evidence
evidence.outcome: Confidence and caveats in LLM answers given counterfactual medical evidence
evidence.effect: Models gave confident, uncaveated answers when the evidence was counterfactual, dangerous or implausible. Exact rates not given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Our evaluation across multiple frontier LLMs on MedCounterFact reveals that in the presence of counterfactual evidence, existing models overwhelmingly accept such "evidence" at face value even when it is dangerous or implausible, and provide confident and uncaveated answers.

evidence.title: Towards Reliable Medical LLMs: Benchmarking and Enhancing Confidence Estimation of Large Language Models in Medical Consultation
evidence.outcome: Reliability of LLM confidence estimates in multi-turn medical consultation as information accumulates
evidence.effect: Medical data amplifies the limitations of token-level and consistency-level confidence methods across 27 methods. The proposed MedConf outperformed state-of-the-art methods on AUROC and Pearson correlation across two LLMs and three datasets, including under information insufficiency.
evidence.quote: We implement and compare 27 representative methods on this benchmark; two key insights emerge: (1) medical data amplifies the inherent limitations of token-level and consistency-level confidence methods, and (2) medical reasoning must be evaluated for both diagnostic accuracy and information completeness.
evidence.sample_unit: consultation cases (three medical datasets; count not reported)

evidence.title: Planner-Auditor Twin: Agentic Discharge Planning with FHIR-Based LLM Planning, Guideline Recall, Optional Caching and Self-Improvement
evidence.outcome: Calibration of LLM confidence estimates (Brier, ECE) and high-confidence misses
evidence.effect: Calibration improved substantially with the auditor loop, with reduced Brier/ECE and fewer high-confidence misses, implying miscalibrated confidence at baseline.
evidence.quote: Calibration improved substantially, with reduced Brier/ECE and fewer high-confidence misses.

evidence.title: Cross-Lingual Empirical Evaluation of Large Language Models for Arabic Medical Tasks
evidence.outcome: Correlation between model-reported confidence/explanations and answer correctness in Arabic and English medical QA
evidence.effect: Model-reported confidence and explanations showed limited correlation with correctness, so stated confidence is an unreliable signal of accuracy.
evidence.quote: Tokenization analysis exposes structural fragmentation in Arabic medical text, while reliability analysis suggests that model-reported confidence and explanations exhibit limited correlation with correctness.

evidence.title: MentalBench: A DSM-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating Psychiatric Diagnostic Capability of Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: LLM confidence calibration when distinguishing psychiatric disorders with overlapping symptoms
evidence.effect: State-of-the-art LLMs performed well on noise-free DSM-5 knowledge queries but struggled to calibrate confidence when distinguishing disorders with overlapping symptoms (no numbers in the abstract).
evidence.quote: Our experiments show that although state-of-the-art LLMs perform well on noise-free queries that probe DSM-5 knowledge, they struggle to calibrate their confidence when distinguishing between disorders with overlapping symptoms.

evidence.title: Calibrated? Not for Everyone: How Sexual Orientation and Religious Markers Distort LLM Accuracy and Confidence in Medical QA
evidence.outcome: Reliability of LLM confidence signals under social identity cues
evidence.effect: Social identity cues affect the reliability of confidence signals, not only predictions, posing a risk in confidence-based clinical workflows.
evidence.quote: Our results demonstrate that the presence of social identity cues does not merely shift predictions; it affects the reliability of confidence signals, posing a significant risk to equitable care and safe deployment in confidence-based clinical workflows.

evidence.title: Safety and accuracy follow different scaling laws in clinical large language models
evidence.outcome: Rate of dangerous overconfidence in LLM answers across deployment conditions
evidence.effect: Dangerous overconfidence was 8.0% closed-book, falling to 1.6% with clean evidence, and remained elevated under standard and agentic RAG.
evidence.quote: Clean evidence produced the strongest improvement, increasing mean accuracy from 73.5% to 94.1%, while reducing high-risk error from 12.0% to 2.6%, contradiction from 12.7% to 2.3%, and dangerous overconfidence from 8.0% to 1.6%.

evidence.title: A Dataset of Robot-Patient and Doctor-Patient Medical Dialogues for Spoken Language Processing Tasks
evidence.outcome: LLM confidence calibration when selecting sentences in medical dialogues
evidence.effect: All three LLMs were highly overconfident in probabilistic predictions whether correct or incorrect; best accuracy was Claude Sonnet 4 at 71.1% (manual transcripts) and 74.7% (automatic transcripts).
evidence.quote: Experimental results reveal that Claude Sonnet 4 is the best in sentence selection, with 71.1% accuracy using manual transcriptions and 74.7% using automatic transcriptions, and that all LLMs are highly overconfident in their probabilistic predictions, regardless of selecting correct or incorrect sentences in medical dialogues.
evidence.sample_unit: hours of speech data (robot-patient and doctor-patient dialogues)

evidence.title: SurgiQ: A Large-Scale Multi-Domain Benchmark for Evaluating Surgical Understanding in Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Model calibration and confident errors on plausible distractors in surgical multiple-choice questions
evidence.effect: Best model reached 68.1% accuracy; smaller models often near 25% random baseline; even strong models made confident mistakes on clinically plausible distractors.
evidence.quote: Calibration and error analysis further show that even strong models make confident mistakes on clinically plausible distractors, motivating more reliable and broader surgical LLM evaluation.

evidence.title: Possible or Definite? A Benchmark for Evaluating Diagnostic Uncertainty Preservation in Clinical Text
evidence.outcome: LLM preservation of diagnostic uncertainty cues across five levels in clinical text revision
evidence.effect: LLMs preserved original uncertainty cues poorly, often less than half the time, and struggled to distinguish adjacent uncertainty levels.
evidence.quote: Our results show that (1) LLMs preserve the original uncertainty cues poorly, often less than half the time; (2) LLMs struggle with nuanced distinctions between adjacent levels.

evidence.title: Aletheia: An Offline-First Clinical Decision Support System for Differential Diagnosis in Low-Resource Healthcare Settings
evidence.outcome: Expected Calibration Error of model confidence in diagnostic outputs
evidence.effect: ECE of 0.275 reported for the fine-tuned model, indicating miscalibrated confidence; Top-1 accuracy 80% (8/10) and Top-3 100% on ten cases.
evidence.quote: The system achieves an Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of 0.275 and passes the Africa Deep Tech Challenge 2026 (ADTC 2026) memory budget constraint of 7168 MB, achieving a peak inference RAM of approximately 3630 MB on the standardised benchmark laptop.

evidence.title: When Confidence Fails: Overconfidence in LLMs under Uncertainty and Missing Clinical Information
evidence.outcome: Alignment of LLM confidence with accuracy under linguistic uncertainty and missing information
evidence.effect: Accuracy degraded with increasing uncertainty while confidence stayed misaligned with accuracy, causing a substantial increase in unsafe confident errors (UCER).
evidence.quote: Our results reveal a consistent failure mode, i.e., although accuracy degrades under increasing uncertainty, model confidence remains misaligned with accuracy.

evidence.title: Large Language Models Show Metacognitive Sensitivity in Medical Reasoning
evidence.outcome: Calibration of LLM confidence against accuracy and evidence strength in diagnostic vignettes
evidence.effect: Accuracy 93.5%, mean confidence 78.4%, AUROC2 0.876. Confidence tracked evidence strength and missing information, but errors in moderate, conflicting AT-NCD cases retained more confidence than accuracy justified.
evidence.quote: However, errors clustered in moderate, conflicting AT-NCD cases, where the model shifted toward DRCI and retained more confidence than empirical accuracy justified.
evidence.sample_unit: trials (45 synthetic vignettes x 3 prompt variants)

evidence.title: Jev in Medicine: A Benchmark Evaluation. Preliminary Results
evidence.outcome: Calibration and confidence-accuracy relationship of model probabilities on MetaMedQA
evidence.effect: Jev ECE 0.063 vs 0.146 for GPT-6 Sol; Jev answers with p>=0.9 (52.9% of questions) were 93.4% accurate, but GPT-6 Sol matched that accuracy at similar coverage. On DiagnosisArena-MCQ, AUROC 0.645 vs 0.768.
evidence.quote: On MetaMedQA, Jev's probabilities were the best calibrated (expected calibration error 0.063 vs 0.146), and its answers with a probability of at least 0.9 (52.9% of questions) were 93.4% accurate, but GPT-6 Sol was as accurate when it accepted a similar proportion of questions.

evidence.title: Across Generations, Sizes, and Types, Large Language Models Poorly Report Self-Confidence in Gastroenterology Clinical Reasoning Tasks
evidence.outcome: Confidence calibration of LLM self-reported certainty on gastroenterology board-style questions (Brier score, AUROC)
evidence.effect: All 48 models showed poor certainty estimation. Even the best-calibrated models had substantial overconfidence (Brier 0.15-0.2, AUROC ~0.6). Models stayed highly certain regardless of question difficulty.
evidence.quote: Even the best-calibrated systems (o1 preview, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet) showed substantial overconfidence (Brier scores 0.15-0.2, AUROC ~0.6).

evidence.title: Evaluating the Impact of Authoritative and Subjective Cues on Large Language Model Reliability for Clinical Inquiries: An Experimental Study
evidence.outcome: Self-rated LLM confidence when accuracy collapsed under authoritative cue
evidence.effect: Accuracy collapsed in the authoritative condition, but self-rated confidence stayed high with no statistical difference from baseline.
evidence.quote: Notably, while accuracy collapsed in the authoritative condition, the models' self-rated confidence remained high, showing no statistical difference from the baseline condition.
evidence.sample_unit: test runs (5 models x 5 scenarios x 10 repetitions)

evidence.title: Probing the Surgical Competence of LLMs: A global health study leveraging AfriMedQA benchmarks
evidence.outcome: Overconfident but incorrect answers from LLMs
evidence.effect: Error analyses revealed overconfident but incorrect answers, along with procedural reasoning failures and omission of local clinical guidelines.
evidence.quote: Error analyses revealed frequent procedural reasoning failures, omission of local clinical guidelines, and overconfident but incorrect answers.
evidence.country: Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya and other African countries (AfriMed-QA benchmark; authored by African medical professors)

evidence.title: AI-generated data contamination erodes pathological variability and diagnostic reliability
evidence.outcome: Decoupling of model confidence from diagnostic accuracy across generations
evidence.effect: Models continue issuing reassuring reports while failing to detect life-threatening pathology; false reassurance rates tripled to 40%.
evidence.quote: Models continue to issue reassuring reports while failing to detect life-threatening pathology, with false reassurance rates tripling to 40%.

evidence.title: Vertical Model Paradox: Systemic Ethical Blind Spots in Domain-Specific Medical AI
evidence.outcome: Professionalism and evidence-based compliance, including warnings for data scarcity or rare diseases
evidence.effect: Domain-specific medical LLMs scored lowest in Professionalism & Evidence-based dimension (78.00%), with generative overconfidence by failing to issue mandatory warnings for data scarcity or rare diseases.
evidence.quote: However, a significant "Vertical Model Paradox" emerged: models specifically fine-tuned on medical corpora (Domain-Specific Medical LLMs) scored lowest in the Professionalism & Evidence-based dimension (78.00%), exhibiting a tendency toward generative overconfidence by failing to issue mandatory warnings for data scarcity or rare diseases.

evidence.title: ConfidentNeuro: Conformal Prediction-Based Uncertainty Quantification for Hallucination Risk Scoring in LLM-Assisted Alzheimer's Clinical Decision Support
evidence.outcome: Calibration of GPT-4o token-level log-probability confidence (ECE)
evidence.effect: GPT-4o was miscalibrated (ECE = 0.213); token-level log probabilities are an unreliable confidence signal in clinical use.
evidence.quote: The calibration audit indicated that GPT-4o is miscalibrated (ECE = 0.213).

evidence.title: Decoupled Transferability of Calibration and Explainability in Cross-Cohort Breast Cancer Survival Prediction
evidence.outcome: calibrated probability transfer
evidence.effect: SEER-fit calibrators increased external ECE two- to three-fold for every model on imputed and complete-case METABRIC cohorts.
evidence.quote: The same SEER-fit calibrators, applied unchanged to METABRIC, increased ECE by a factor of two to three for every model on both the imputed and complete-case external cohorts, a direct consequence of the base-rate shift from 84.7% to 42.1% alive.
evidence.country: United States and United Kingdom/Canada (SEER and METABRIC cohorts)

evidence.title: Performance evaluation and benchmarking across 16 large language models on a comprehensive real-world emergency department triage data set
evidence.outcome: Calibration of verbalized confidence in LLM triage outputs
evidence.effect: Most models showed systematic overconfidence, with expected calibration errors from verbalized confidence ranging from 0.099 to 0.355.
evidence.quote: Most models demonstrated moderate or lower agreement and systematic overconfidence, with expected calibration errors (ECE) based on verbalized confidence ranging from 0.099 to 0.355.

evidence.title: A Systematic Exploration of LLM Behavior for EHR Phenotyping
evidence.outcome: Calibration of LLM self-reported confidence against accuracy in phenotype predictions
evidence.effect: Self-confidence was only moderately informative. High-confidence predictions were more accurate, but larger models showed systematic overconfidence.
evidence.quote: Self-confidence calibration was only moderately informative: high-confidence predictions were more accurate, but larger models exhibited systematic overconfidence.

evidence.title: Comparative Performance of General-Purpose Large Language Models and a Specialized Clinical AI Tool on OKAP-Style Ophthalmology Questions
evidence.outcome: Calibration and confidence-based discrimination of LLM outputs
evidence.effect: Gemini-Pro-3 best calibration; Claude-Opus-4.6 and ChatGPT-5.4-Pro strongest confidence-based discrimination; calibration varied across models.
evidence.quote: Gemini-Pro-3 showed the best calibration, whereas Claude-Opus-4.6 and ChatGPT-5.4-Pro showed the strongest confidence-based discrimination.

evidence.title: Intent Drift in LLM-Assisted BCI Communication: An In-Silico Benchmark Under Simulated Decoder Corruption
evidence.outcome: Calibration of model confidence versus faithfulness of BCI text corrections
evidence.effect: Confidence discriminated correct from incorrect outputs (AUROC 0.83) but 28.4% of high-confidence outputs were not faithful.
evidence.quote: Model confidence distinguished correct from incorrect outputs reasonably well (AUROC 0.83) but overstated its own reliability: 28.4% of high-confidence outputs were not faithful.

evidence.title: RheumBench: A Specialist-Validated Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Rheumatology
evidence.outcome: Calibration of self-reported system confidence against diagnostic accuracy (Brier score)
evidence.effect: Self-reported confidence was generally high, and all systems were systematically overconfident; the lowest Brier score was 0.203 (Claude Fable 5).
evidence.quote: Self-reported system confidence was generally high and diagnostic calibration analyses showed systematic overconfidence for all systems, with the lowest Brier score of 0.203 (Claude Fable 5).
evidence.sample_unit: clinical cases (70 diagnostic, 30 management; 1,020 rubric criteria)

evidence.title: Condence, Calibration, and Abstention in Small Open-Weight Language Models on Psychiatric Knowledge Questions: A Cross-Domain Replication
evidence.outcome: Calibration and error-detection quality of verbalized confidence (AUROC, ECE)
evidence.effect: Verbalized confidence AUROC 0.490-0.645 (4.3B indistinguishable from chance); ECE 0.148-0.378 versus 0.041-0.141 reported for proprietary frontier models on the same benchmark family.
evidence.quote: Verbalized condence remains poorly informative about correctness as a ranking signal (AUROC 0.4900.645; one model, the 4.3B, is statistically indistin- guishable from chance) and severely miscalibrated in the aggregate sense (ECE 0.1480.378, well above the 0.0410.141 range Boie et al. report for proprietary frontier models on the same under- lying benchmark family).

evidence.title: Performance of GPT-4 on the American College of Radiology In-Service Examination
evidence.outcome: Model-stated confidence for correct versus incorrect answers
evidence.effect: Confidence was 87.1% for correct answers and 84.0% for incorrect answers (p = 0.012), so confidence was high even when wrong. Overall accuracy was 58.5%.
evidence.quote: GPT-4 showed significantly higher (p = 0.012) confidence for correct answers (87.1%) compared to incorrect (84.0%).

evidence.title: Exploring the Capabilities of ChatGPT in Women’s Health
evidence.outcome: Whether ChatGPT's self-assessed confidence and entropy distinguished correct from incorrect answers
evidence.effect: Median confidence was 70% for correct answers and for incorrect answers judged correct (p<0.001). Entropy was identical for correct and incorrect responses (median 1.46, IQR 0.44–1.77).
evidence.quote: Entropy values were identical for correct and incorrect responses (median 1.46, IQR 0.44–1.77), indicating no discernible distinction in ChatGPT’s prediction certainty.

evidence.title: Assessing the Performance of Plugin-Integrated ChatGPT-4 in the German Medical Board Examination: An Experimental Study on the Advancements and Limitations of Modern AI Modelling Approaches
evidence.outcome: Ability of GPT models to express calibrated uncertainty in answers to board exam questions
evidence.effect: Models could assess uncertainty in their responses but were overconfident; a new 'confidence accuracy' metric was developed. No numeric values are given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Moreover, the models could assess the uncertainty in their responses, albeit exhibiting overconfidence.

evidence.title: Comparative Evaluation of LLMs in Clinical Oncology
evidence.outcome: Overconfidence in LLM self-appraised confidence scores
evidence.effect: Study reports examples of overconfidence and consistent inaccuracies across all LLMs, despite confidence self-appraisal being useful for identifying higher-accuracy subgroups.
evidence.quote: Although this performance is impressive, all LLMs continue to have clinically significant error rates, including examples of overconfidence and consistent inaccuracies.

evidence.title: Why implementing machine learning algorithms in the clinic is not a plug-and-play solution: a simulation study of a machine learning algorithm for acute leukaemia subtype diagnosis
evidence.outcome: False confident diagnosis labels
evidence.effect: ALL: 0/104 confidently ALL; 1 ALL patient confidently APL and 9 ALL patients confidently AML.
evidence.quote: Using these cutoffs, not a single ALL case of UME was classified as ‘confident ALL’ (N = 0/104), while 1 ALL patient was classified ‘confident APL’ and 9 ALL patients as ‘confident AML’ ( Table 2 a).

evidence.title: Uncertainty estimation in diagnosis generation from large language models: next-word probability is not pre-test probability
evidence.outcome: Quality of LLM uncertainty estimates (verbalized confidence, token logits) for pre-test diagnostic probability
evidence.effect: Verbalized Confidence and Token Logits underperformed the XGB baseline; LLM Embedding+XGB came closest. Authors conclude LLMs fall short of reliable pre-test probability estimation and need improved calibration.
evidence.quote: LLM Embedding+XGB showed the closest performance to the XGB baseline, while Verbalized Confidence and Token Logits underperformed.

evidence.title: Performance of GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 in the Polish Infectious Diseases Specialty Exam
evidence.outcome: Difference in model self-reported confidence between correct and incorrect answers
evidence.effect: Both models showed statistically significant differences in confidence between correct and incorrect answers, with higher confidence for correct answers and lower confidence for incorrect ones.
evidence.quote: For both AI models, a statistically significant difference was observed in the confidence levels between correct and incorrect answers, with higher confidence reported for correctly answered questions and lower confidence for incorrectly answered ones.

evidence.title: Five advanced chatbots solving European Diploma in Radiology (EDiR) text-based questions: differences in performance and consistency
evidence.outcome: Self-reported confidence (0-10) versus accuracy of chatbot answers
evidence.effect: Confidence was high for all models (8.2-9.0) while scores ranged 0.54-0.84. Lower-scoring models reported somewhat lower confidence, but Gemini (0.54) still reported 8.2 ± 1.6.
evidence.quote: A self-reported confidence in answering the questions was 9.0 ± 0.9 for Claude 3.5 Sonnet followed by ChatGPT-4o (8.7 ± 1.1), compared to ChatGPT-4o-mini (8.2 ± 1.3), Copilot (8.2 ± 2.2), and Gemini (8.2 ± 1.6, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Token Probabilities to Mitigate Large Language Models Overconfidence in Answering Medical Questions: Quantitative Study
evidence.outcome: Whether LLM self-expressed confidence predicts response accuracy on medical exam questions (AUROC)
evidence.effect: Chatbots expressed uniformly high confidence (90-100) yet self-rated confidence AUROC was only 0.52-0.68. Token probability AUROC was 0.71-0.87, and all models showed imperfect calibration with a trend toward overconfidence.
evidence.quote: However, expressed confidence failed to predict response accuracy (AUROC ranging from 0.52, 95% CI 0.50-0.53 for Phi-3-Mini to 0.68, 95% CI 0.65-0.71 for GPT-4o).

evidence.title: Evaluation of reliability, repeatability, and confidence of ChatGPT for screening, monitoring, and treatment of interstitial lung disease in patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases
evidence.outcome: Overconfidence: high confidence scores assigned to incorrect answers
evidence.effect: Overconfidence percentage was 100% (22 of 22) for GPT-4o and 22.7% (10 of 44) for GPT-4o mini (P < .01).
evidence.quote: Furthermore, the overconfidence percentage (confidence score of ≥8 assigned to incorrect answers) was 100% (22 of 22) for GPT-4o and 22.7% (10 of 44) for GPT-4o mini, respectively (P < .01).

evidence.title: Automated real-time assessment of intracranial hemorrhage detection AI using an ensembled monitoring model (EMM)
evidence.outcome: False confidence when the confidence estimator agrees with an incorrect primary AI prediction
evidence.effect: EMM showed full agreement with an incorrect primary prediction in 138 cases (4%), mainly subtle hemorrhages or hemorrhage mimics, which could instill false confidence.
evidence.quote: Of particular concern are instances where EMM fails simultaneously with the primary model while indicating complete consensus, as this could instill false confidence in clinicians and potentially increase misdiagnosis risk.

evidence.title: Comparison of GPT-4o With Human Performance in the Polish Vascular Surgery Specialty Examination
evidence.outcome: Correlation between model self-reported confidence rating and answer correctness on exam questions
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-4o answered 88 of 120 correctly (73.3%), but its self-reported confidence levels did not largely correlate with accuracy, so it could not consistently predict its own performance.
evidence.quote: The model's self-reported confidence levels did not largely correlate with its response accuracy.

evidence.title: Limitations of large language models in clinical problem-solving arising from inflexible reasoning
evidence.outcome: LLM confidence calibration relative to accuracy on mARC-QA
evidence.effect: Uncertainty estimation analyses indicate LLMs exhibit overconfidence in their answers despite limited accuracy.
evidence.quote: In addition, uncertainty estimation analyses indicate that LLMs exhibit overconfidence in their answers, despite their limited accuracy.

evidence.title: Benchmarking large language models on the United States medical licensing examination for clinical reasoning and medical licensing scenarios
evidence.outcome: Model overconfidence and hallucination observed in USMLE question answering
evidence.effect: Models exhibited overconfidence and hallucinations despite high accuracy (DeepSeek 93% on Step 2 CK); universal failures rare (≤1.60%) but concentrated in multimodal and quantitative tasks.
evidence.quote: Despite encouraging accuracy, models exhibited overconfidence and hallucinations, underscoring the need for human oversight.

evidence.title: Comparative evaluation of large language models on multiple-choice and image-based rheumatology questions
evidence.outcome: Self-reported confidence versus accuracy on image-based rheumatology questions
evidence.effect: Confidence stayed high (7-10 for MCQs, 8-10 for image questions) although image accuracy ranged from 16% (Claude) to 56% (Gemini) and hallucinations occurred in 40% (Gemini) to 84% (Claude) of image responses.
evidence.quote: High confidence in incorrect image responses and frequent hallucinations highlight the need for caution when integrating these tools into clinical education or decision-making.

evidence.title: Performance of the ChatGPT-5 Language Model in Solving a Specialty Examination in Balneology and Physical Medicine
evidence.outcome: Correlation between ChatGPT-5 self-declared confidence (1-5) and answer correctness on exam questions
evidence.effect: Correctness was positively correlated with self-assessed confidence (p = 0.029); confidence differences between clinical and theoretical questions were not significant (Mann-Whitney p = 0.07).
evidence.quote: Answer correctness was positively correlated with the model's self-assessed confidence level (p = 0.029): the higher the declared confidence, the greater the likelihood of a correct response.

evidence.title: Reasoning-optimised large language models reach near-expert accuracy on board-style orthopaedic exams: A multi-model comparison on 702 multiple-choice questions
evidence.venue: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
evidence.outcome: Calibration of model confidence (ECE, Brier score)

commentary.bottom_line: Across 85 studies, mostly offline and level 4, uncertainty signals tended to separate correct from incorrect AI outputs and supported deferral or abstention, but no study measured whether calibrated uncertainty expression reduces patient harm in real care. How clinicians respond to uncertainty displays varied by display format, so developers and evaluators should test the display as well as the calibration.

perspectives.view: One level 2 real-deployment study found mean confidence of 0.97 for correct versus 0.81 for incorrect medication and lab mappings. The rest are level 4, mostly offline, and report surrogate outcomes such as error separation. Uncertain nodules had an AUC of 0.62 versus 0.93 for certain ones. One study found entropy ran in the opposite direction, which lowers consistency.

In chest X-rays, AI accuracy was 0.596 on images the AI flagged as uncertain, while physicians reached 0.698 on those images, which suggests deferral may catch errors. An uncertainty-acknowledgement prompt lowered hallucination rates from 65.9% to 44.2% without eliminating them. In a hazard study, one model conveyed high confidence on 100% of responses at 45-65% accuracy.

In a 192-participant trial, token-level uncertainty displays increased agreement with the AI. Relation-level displays reduced users' external verification. In a separate trial of 64 clinicians, trust was lower when the AI performed worst. These findings suggest that display format may shape clinician behavior as much as calibration does, and both trials were simulated.

Uncertainty thresholds shift work to human reviewers. Reviewing fewer than 10% of patients captured all extraction errors for two conditions, but capturing all seizure errors required reviewing 19.6%. Certainty thresholds raised accuracy above 90%, but fewer than half of items were then covered automatically. Abstention rose from 9.6% to 22% as the required confidence increased.

A regulatory discussion paper asks whether a device defers when uncertain without over-deferring, and FUTURE-AI calls for calibrated uncertainty estimates. Across models built on the same data, the share of cases flagged as uncertain ranged from 0.3% to 59.9%. This spread suggests that any standard would need to address the amount of deferral as well as coverage.

Three tests used non-English clinical text, from Finland, Switzerland, and Japan. One of these found that the entropy signal ran counter to expectations after translation. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Whether uncertainty signals hold up across these patient groups is therefore unknown.

In a real deployment of 2,035 patient conversations, a chatbot gave confident answers that filled gaps in its evidence rather than signaling uncertainty. No practice test measured patient understanding, trust, or whether patients reached a human after an uncertainty flag.

commentary.research_gap: No study tested calibrated uncertainty expression in live clinical use with outcomes such as intercepted errors, clinician verification behavior, or patient harm. Evaluations of generative model outputs and of patient-facing uncertainty messages remain sparse. Head-to-head comparisons of display formats in real workflows are also needed.
commentary.underserved_note: Three tests used non-English source text from European and Japanese settings, and one included older adults. None included Medicaid, safety-net, US limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is unknown whether calibration and error flagging perform equally for these groups, or whether patients in these groups understand uncertainty messages.
